# Isochronic Passage Chart

> An interactive globe showing expected door-to-door travel time from each of
> its departure cities (the list is `origins` in index.json) to every land area
> on Earth, combining scheduled air routes, rail from OpenStreetMap route
> relations, ferry crossings, and a road-speed model whose four middle road
> classes are fitted to 2,998 real driving journeys sampled from the Google
> Routes API (calibration only; nothing from it reaches the site, and no
> commercial flight data is used anywhere), the roadless and local classes
> keeping published-figure defaults, with check-in, border-control and
> transfer penalties.
> Air times are fitted to 107,366 ADS-B flight legs. Named after Francis
> Galton's "Isochronic Passage Chart for Travellers" (1881), the first
> published travel-time map.

## What the numbers mean

Times are expected door-to-door minutes: the way to the airport or station,
check-in and security, border control where a zone is crossed, and the journey
out of the arrival airport are all in the figure. They are drawn in 37 bands on
a geometric ladder from under 30 minutes to over 72 hours; the band edges are
`bandEdgesMin` in index.json. A departure is treated as planned, so the first
service is not waited for. An onward flight connection is charged the minimum
connection time or the expected wait for the next service, whichever is
longer, capped at the cost of leaving and re-entering the terminal (55 minutes at a
small airport, 1 h 40 at a large one). A ferry leg IS charged an expected wait --
half the interval between sailings, from the route's own OpenStreetMap
timetable where it carries one and otherwise from a headway fitted to eight
published crossings -- on top of the sailing and the terminal time. Rail legs
carry no wait: they are charged running time, a per-stop allowance, and 20
minutes for reaching the platform and leaving the arrival station. Running
time comes from one of six service tiers, 74 km/h for a commuter service up
to 215 km/h for a high-speed one, plus a separate 20 km/h tier for heritage
and tourist lines, fitted against OSM `duration` tags. A route's tier is
read from its own OpenStreetMap `service` tag WHERE IT CARRIES ONE: about a
quarter of route relations do not, and those fall to a general-purpose
default. The model's largest known error is the Tohoku Shinkansen at about
10 h against a published 3 h 10, and the larger part of that IS speed: all
three Shinkansen relations carry no `service` tag at all, so all three are
priced at the default, 82 km/h -- the `highspeed` tag sits on the track
segments rather than on the route, so the route reads as ordinary. Pricing
them as high-speed instead would take about 5 h off, 70% of the error. The
stop sequence is the second and smaller cause: the relation lists 21 station
calls where the fastest train makes about six, and the per-stop allowance for
the other fifteen is 37 minutes, 9% of the error. Corrected both ways the
journey would still come out near 4 h. Express services running on
all-stations relations are over-stated the same way.

## How it is computed

A single-source Dijkstra runs over one multi-modal graph per departure city.
The ground is 4,091,715 H3 resolution-6 land cells (about 36 km2, 6.5 km
across), refined to resolution 7 (5.2 km2, 2.4 km across) wherever the road
network reaches secondary grade or a metropolitan area lies. Ground movement
between adjacent cells is charged at a per-cell speed derived from GRIP4
road-density rasters, halved inside cities. Flights connect airport pairs taken
from Wikipedia's "Airlines and destinations" tables, resolved to IATA codes
through Wikidata property P238, with block time modelled from great-circle
distance. Rail runs stop to stop along OpenStreetMap route relations; ferries
along OpenStreetMap ferry ways, charging the sailing, the terminal time and
the expected wait for the next departure. The per-cell result is dissolved into bands
and shipped as PMTiles at four levels of detail, plus per-origin binary arrays
of time, arrival airport, surface mode and rail station on a resolution-4 hover
grid. The arrays are little-endian uint16, one value per hover cell: `.bin`
(time, 181 KB), `.air.bin` (arrival airport, 181 KB), `.rail.bin` (rail
station, 181 KB) and `.modes.bin` (1.09 MB, six channels per cell).
`hover_cells.bin` (726 KB) gives their ordering: the sorted resolution-4 cell
ids as little-endian uint64.

A second, finer reading tier ships alongside: `{slug}.r6.bin` (9.55 MB), the
time array at resolution 6 -- the grid the bands are painted from, so the
number printed under the pointer is the value of the cell the map outlines
rather than an average over a cell about 45 km across. It is laid out as
fixed-width blocks of 343 slots keyed by the resolution-3 parent, so the slot
within a block is arithmetic and no per-origin cell list is needed;
`reading_parents.bin` (117 KB) ships that parent ordering once for the whole
site. The tier is fetched lazily, after the first paint and never on the boot
path, and it is skipped entirely when the browser reports Save-Data. A build
whose index.json carries no `readingRes` has no such files, and the page falls
back to the resolution-4 array and says so under the number. In refined areas
the paint is still finer than the reading: where the solver split a cell the
map draws its seven resolution-7 children, and the reading is the value of the
CENTRE child -- not an average over the seven. That is the same "what a pointer
at this spot means" rule the resolution-4 tier uses, so the two tiers cannot
disagree about which child speaks for a cell.

## Known limits

- The air model is a regression on 107,366 legs with a held-out MEAN absolute
  error of about 9 minutes on the airborne portion (`holdout_mae_min` in
  calibration.toml; `calibrate/fit.py` takes `.mean()`, not a median), and a
  signed bias by distance -- those bucket figures ARE medians:
  +2 min at 150-400 km, +3 at 400-800, 0 at 800-1500, -1 at 1500-3000, +6 at
  3000-6000. Figures are printed to the minute; none is accurate to the minute.
- That fit is VALID ONLY BETWEEN 150 AND 6000 km. Beyond 6000 km it is
  extrapolation: ocean receiver coverage trips the 900 s split rule, so only 2
  of 107,366 legs exceed it. Intercontinental readings are therefore the least
  certain, and long-haul varies by about an hour on winds alone. Treat
  10,000 km+ as approximate.
- Flight frequency is a gravity model hand-fitted to two anchor routes, not
  published timetables.
- Rail legs carry no waiting time.
- The ferry headway prior is fitted to eight published crossings and is wide:
  a factor of about 2 at one sigma against those anchors, and against 326
  independent OpenStreetMap `interval` tags a factor of 3.6, with the bias
  changing sign at about 150 km. Distance alone cannot tell a remote lifeline
  route from a busy short-sea one. Where a crossing carries an `interval` tag
  the tag is used and the prior is not consulted. The error is documented
  rather than corrected; calibration.toml tabulates it.
- Every departure reaches at least 90 % of non-Antarctic land (a build gate);
  land with no modelled route is drawn in the grey the legend names.
- The build that is live may lag the code: `solveRes`, `origins` and
  `modeDetail` in index.json describe what is actually served. This bears on
  the ferry wait above in particular: a build made before that model charges
  no ferry wait at all, and `modeDetail.ferry` is written by the build, so it
  states which of the two is being served.

## Data sources

- OurAirports (public domain) - airport locations and service status
- Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0) - airline route network
- Wikidata (CC0) - IATA code resolution
- OpenStreetMap (ODbL) - coastlines drawn on the map; rail route relations and ferry ways
- GRIP4 (CC0) - global road density; itself built partly from OpenStreetMap
- Natural Earth (public domain) - land mask, country borders, populated places behind the urban mask
- GeoNames (CC BY 4.0) - departure cities and the place names under the cursor (cities15000)
- HydroLAKES (CC BY 4.0) - lake outlines drawn on the map
- adsb.lol (ODbL) - observed flights behind the fitted cruise speed and climb/descent penalty

At runtime the page calls two external services: OpenStreetMap's Nominatim
for address search and click-to-address (only when a search is submitted or a
point is clicked), and Google Analytics for page-view counting. Where the
build enables it, the time from the exact point a departure marker was dragged
to is computed on demand by this site's own server (`/api/solve`); the map
itself is still measured from the nearest charted city. Everything else is
computed in the browser from files on this site.

## Links

- [Chart](https://worldmap.atik.kr/): the map itself
- [Machine-readable index](https://worldmap.atik.kr/index.json): origins, band
  edges, resolutions, mode descriptions and source attribution for the build
  that is actually being served

## Disclaimer

For reference only. All figures are estimates computed from open data and a simplified model. They carry no warranty of accuracy, are not travel advice, and must not be relied on for any journey, booking, or decision. The author accepts no liability for any use.

A departure city can be opened directly with `?from=<slug>` (the slugs are the `origins[].slug` values in index.json); the page keeps the address bar in step with the selected departure.
